strengths: The paper addresses an important visual-navigation problem: continuous control in narrow, cluttered, and dynamic environments using surround-view RGB observations. Integrating specialized depth-based RL teachers into one RGB policy is a coherent and practically motivated approach.

Table I reports substantial simulation improvements over the strongest evaluated baseline, NavDP: success rates increase from 18% to 71% for squeezing, 27% to 68% for avoiding, and 23% to 47% in the mixed scene. Collision rates also improve substantially.

The ablations provide useful evidence for online refinement and diverse expert supervision. Table II controls the total data quantity across single-expert and mixed-expert VLA models, while Figure 6 compares data-balancing strategies with equal samples per iteration.

Deployment on a physical quadruped at approximately 7 Hz, including demonstrations involving thin obstacles and confined passages, establishes practical feasibility. The manuscript also provides useful information about model components, data volumes, training hardware, and inference hardware.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not isolate the proposed learning contribution. MM-Nav receives four camera views, whereas the evaluated baselines retain their original front-facing configurations; the paper itself attributes many failures to this disparity. There is no single-view MM-Nav ablation or comparable surround-view baseline. Likewise, no controlled experiment establishes the contribution of the language backbone or VQA co-training relative to a simpler visual policy trained on the same data. These omissions matter because no contribution type is declared, so I assess the paper as Algorithms/General.

The central claim of robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer is supported only by qualitative demonstrations. No real-world trial counts, success/collision rates, quantitative baseline comparisons, or systematic failure analysis are reported. The images establish feasibility but cannot substantiate the abstract's characterization of extensive real-world validation or reliable operation around thin and transparent obstacles.

The algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental: the method combines established multi-view perception, pretrained visual/language models, continuous-action regression, policy distillation, and DAgger-style supervision. The most distinct element is the WTT-based sampling heuristic, but its evaluation remains limited. The 'unbalanced' sampling distribution is not specified, and Figure 6 provides no repeated-run uncertainty to establish the claimed faster and more stable learning.

The evidence supports benefits from diverse training data more strongly than the claimed synergistic mechanism. Table II does not include a VLA student distilled from the Mixed-RL teacher, which would help distinguish specialization of teachers from exposure to diverse scenes. The explanation that Mixed-RL underperforms because of capacity limits is not tested. Moreover, the final student does not exceed the squeezing teacher in success rate (71% versus 73%); the claimed advantage in WTT should be distinguished clearly from superiority across navigation metrics.

Evaluation coverage and reporting limit confidence in generalization. Tests use three fixed capability-specific scenes and one mixed scene, with 100 episodes per method and no training-seed variability or confidence intervals. The separation between scenes used to update sampling proportions and those used for final evaluation is unclear. Mixed-scene success remains 47%, with 26% collisions, warranting a more qualified account of robustness.

Several details needed for reproduction are missing, including precise reward functions and success thresholds, optimizer and fine-tuning settings, replay-buffer retention, baseline adaptation, and how relative goal coordinates are obtained during physical deployment. There is also a minor architecture inconsistency: Equation (4) with eight timesteps implies 176 visual tokens, rather than the stated 192. These reporting issues are secondary to the experimental concerns but should be corrected.

strengths: The paper addresses an important visual-navigation problem: continuous control in narrow spaces and around dynamic obstacles using surround-view RGB observations. Evaluated as Algorithms/General, the integration of specialized depth-based RL teachers, a multi-view VLA student, and capability-dependent data aggregation is coherent and practically motivated.

Table I reports substantial simulation improvements over the evaluated baselines. Compared with NavDP, success rates increase from 18% to 71% for squeezing, 27% to 68% for avoiding, and 23% to 47% in the mixed scene, with lower collision rates.

The ablations provide useful evidence. Figure 6 compares balanced and unbalanced aggregation with equal sample counts, while Table II compares single-expert and mixed-expert training with equal total data. These results support the usefulness of diverse supervision and adaptive sampling.

The physical robot demonstrations involving thin obstacles, tight passages, and moving obstructions provide encouraging evidence of transfer. The manuscript also reports training resources, dataset sizes, and deployment hardware, including approximately 7 Hz operation.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not isolate the proposed learning contribution. MM-Nav receives four camera views, whereas the external baselines retain their original, restricted fields of view; the paper explicitly attributes several baseline failures to this difference. These comparisons establish a system-level advantage but cannot distinguish improvements from sensing coverage, model capacity, training data, and multi-expert learning. A matched-input baseline and ablations of surround-view sensing and the pretrained VLA backbone are particularly important.

The central claim of robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer is supported only qualitatively. Figures 1 and 5 show selected demonstrations, but no real-world success/collision statistics, trial counts, quantitative baseline comparisons, or failure analysis are reported. The source and accuracy of the real-world relative-goal estimate are also unspecified. Consequently, the evidence establishes feasibility more convincingly than reliable deployment.

The incremental contribution over the acknowledged ingredients—multi-view perception, pretrained VLA models, privileged policy distillation, and DAgger—is insufficiently established. The capability-balancing rule is a plausible heuristic, but its comparison uses an incompletely specified 'unbalanced' sampling policy. Table II also lacks a VLA student distilled from the mixed RL teacher, which would help determine whether specialized teachers are essential beyond exposure to diverse training scenes.

The strength and scope of several conclusions exceed the evidence. In Table II, the mixed VLA improves over the reaching and avoiding specialists but does not exceed the squeezing specialist's success rate (71% versus 73%); the separate WTT superiority claim is not accompanied by tabulated teacher WTT results. Broader claims of robust navigation should also acknowledge 47% success and 26% collisions in the mixed scene. Better cross-task performance supports useful transfer, but does not by itself prove the proposed explanation of synergistic representations.

Evaluation and reproduction details remain incomplete. Testing uses a small collection of custom fixed scenes, without sufficient specification of scene generation, episode sampling, or a separate validation set for selecting data proportions and stopping iterations. Results lack repeated training runs or uncertainty estimates, which matters especially for modest ablation differences. Important training details are omitted, including optimizer settings, trainable modules, exact reward definitions, and replay-buffer retention across iterations. These gaps, together with the missing controlled and quantitative real-world evidence, favor rejection despite the promising simulation results.

strengths: The paper addresses an important visual-navigation problem: continuous control in narrow, cluttered, and dynamic environments using surround-view RGB observations. The integration of specialized depth-based teachers, a multi-view VLA student, and capability-balanced online imitation is coherent and practically motivated.

Simulation improvements are substantial. Across 100 episodes per scene, MM-Nav achieves 71% success on squeezing and 68% on avoiding, versus NavDP’s 18% and 27%; mixed-scene success improves from 23% to 47% (Table I). Collision rates also decrease considerably.

The ablations provide useful evidence for the training design. Table II controls the total data amount when comparing single-expert and mixed-expert students, supporting the value of combining capabilities. Figure 6 compares balancing strategies at equal per-iteration sample budgets and shows benefits for squeezing and avoiding.

Deployment on a physical quadruped at approximately 7 Hz, including demonstrations involving thin obstacles and tight clearances, provides encouraging feasibility evidence. The manuscript clearly explains the main training stages and attributes the principal pretrained models and learning methods.
weaknesses: The main comparisons do not isolate the proposed learning contribution. MM-Nav uses four cameras, while the baselines retain their original configurations and are explicitly disadvantaged by their limited field of view. There is no single-view MM-Nav ablation or comparable surround-view baseline. Ablations of the pretrained language backbone and VQA co-training are also absent, leaving the claimed role of VLA generalization insufficiently established.

The claim of extensive, robust zero-shot real-world transfer rests on qualitative demonstrations. No real-world trial counts, success or collision rates, repeated-run variability, or quantitative baseline comparisons are reported. These omissions are consequential because sim-to-real robustness is a central motivation and claimed contribution.

The experimental protocol needs stronger separation and specification. The paper uses three fixed capability-specific test scenes but does not explain whether separate validation scenes determine sampling proportions and convergence. Training seeds and uncertainty estimates are absent. The 47% success and 26% collision rate in the mixed scene also limit the breadth of the robustness claim.

The evidence supports complementary training benefits more strongly than the proposed explanations. The final student does not exceed every specialist in success rate: squeezing reaches 71% versus 73% for its RL teacher. Figure 4 claims superiority in WTT, but numerical teacher–student WTT comparisons are not tabulated. Attributing the mixed RL teacher’s poorer performance to capacity limitations, or student gains to specific shared geometric representations, remains speculative.

Reproduction would require missing details, including optimizer settings and trainable components, exact reward terms, simulator distributions and goal tolerance, baseline adaptation procedures, and replay-buffer handling. The source of the robot’s relative goal coordinates is also unspecified. A smaller reporting inconsistency is that the stated eight-frame tokenization yields 176 visual tokens under Equation 4, rather than the reported 192.

Overall, under the default Algorithms/General category, the promising system and substantial simulation gains make this a close decision. However, confounded comparisons and insufficient quantitative transfer evidence leave a slight preference for rejection; these affect the scientific case more than presentation alone.

strengths: The paper addresses an important visual navigation problem: continuous control in narrow passages and dynamic clutter using RGB observations. Under Algorithms/General, the contribution is primarily a coherent integration of specialized RL supervision, multi-view perception, VQA co-training, and adaptive data collection.

The public benchmark results are strong. Table 1 reports average success rates of 88.1% for multi-view MM-Nav and 83.3% for its single-view variant, versus 72.2% for SIDP. The single-view comparison provides useful evidence that the improvement is not solely attributable to additional cameras.

The custom benchmark evaluates complementary navigation capabilities and a mixed environment with changed materials. MM-Nav substantially improves success and collision rates over the evaluated baselines, including 71% squeezing success versus 18% for NavDP.

The ablations cover several important design choices. Figure 7 compares adaptive sampling against an equal-sample-budget alternative, while Table 3 supports the benefit of combining expert capabilities. The real-world VQA ablation includes 20 trials per model in each of four scenarios and shows substantial improvements.

Deployment on a physical quadruped at approximately 7 Hz demonstrates practical feasibility. The appendix provides useful expert-training details, including environment construction, reward coefficients, PPO settings, and training hardware.
weaknesses: The distinctive algorithmic contribution is relatively modest, and its isolation remains incomplete. Most components build on established methods; the main new training mechanism is WTT-based capability sampling. Figure 7 does not precisely define the 'unbalanced' sampling distribution or report variation across training seeds. Final gains of 6 points in squeezing and 9 in avoiding are promising, but 100 evaluation episodes without uncertainty estimates provide limited evidence for the claimed stability and convergence benefits.

The custom benchmark comparisons conflate training methodology with observation coverage, model capacity, and control configuration. The manuscript explicitly attributes baseline failures to their front-facing cameras, but does not evaluate its own single-view variant on these challenging scenes. Table 3 also lacks a student distilled from the mixed RL teacher under the same training procedure, which would better isolate the advantage of specialized teachers.

Real-world evidence supports feasibility more strongly than broad robustness. The four scenarios are selected from a larger set of deployments, without reporting selection criteria or aggregate outcomes. Comparisons are limited to removing VQA, and collision rates, intervention rules, goal-localization inputs, and latency variability are unspecified. The reported 7 Hz requires an external RTX 5090 server, limiting conclusions about onboard deployment.

Several numerical claims need reconciliation. Section 4.4 claims a greater-than-20% VQA-related performance drop in both public-benchmark splits, which Table 1 does not support under either listed full-model comparison. Table 3 shows the student below the squeezing teacher in success rate, 71% versus 73%, so statements about surpassing all experts must specify the metric. Also, 500k initial navigation steps plus four 200k-step iterations total 1.3 million, rather than the advertised 1.5 million; the corresponding VQA counts total 260k rather than 300k. These discrepancies do not erase the gains, but weaken reporting confidence.

Reproducibility of the student pipeline is insufficiently specified despite the detailed RL appendix. Missing information includes student optimization settings, frozen versus trainable components, replay of previously collected data, the exact VQA subset and sampling procedure, and whether capability-balancing measurements use a separate validation set. Figure 6 also lacks sufficient definition of its gap-axis statistic and projection procedure to establish quantitative representation alignment.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant visual-navigation problem: learning continuous control for narrow passages and dynamic obstacles from RGB observations. The integration of specialized privileged RL teachers, surround-view perception, and VQA co-training is technically coherent.

The public-benchmark results are strong. In Table 1, even the single-view model achieves 79.9%/86.7% success on Home/Commercial, compared with 63.2%/81.2% for SIDP. Thus, the reported improvement cannot be explained solely by additional cameras.

The experimental coverage includes a public benchmark, capability-specific simulation environments, a mixed environment, and physical-robot trials. The VQA ablation includes 20 real-world trials per scenario and provides meaningful evidence that co-training improves transfer.

The appendix provides useful details about expert environments, reward functions, and PPO training. The manuscript also attributes its principal pretrained components and methodological building blocks.
weaknesses: The central multi-expert contribution is not sufficiently isolated. Table 3 compares specialized-data students with a student receiving all capabilities, but broader capability coverage naturally favors the latter. Although a mixed-scene RL teacher is evaluated, there is no matched VLA student distilled from that teacher. Consequently, the experiments do not establish how much benefit comes specifically from multiple specialized teachers rather than diverse data, student capacity, and iterative supervision.

The capability-balancing evidence remains incomplete. Figure 7 includes a useful equal-budget comparison, but the sampling policy called 'unbalanced' is not precisely specified, and no variation across training seeds is reported. The final squeezing and avoiding improvements are 6 and 9 percentage points over 100 evaluation episodes, respectively. These results suggest a benefit but provide limited support for the stronger claims about stability and convergence.

Real-world evidence supports feasibility more convincingly than robust comparative performance. The four scenarios are explicitly selected from broader deployments, and the only quantitative comparator is the model without VQA. There are no real-world comparisons against existing navigation policies or detailed collision, intervention, and latency statistics. Success is only 55% on thin-wire avoidance and 70% on pedestrian avoidance, which warrants a more qualified account of reliability.

Several quantitative statements require reconciliation. Section 4.4 claims that removing VQA causes a drop exceeding 20% in both public-benchmark splits, which Table 1 does not support for Home under either relative or percentage-point interpretations. The observation configuration of the no-VQA row is also unspecified. Figure 4's final WTT values differ from Table 2 without explaining whether they use different evaluation sets. These issues weaken the interpretation of important ablations, although they do not erase the headline gains.

Reproducibility is substantially stronger for the RL teachers than for the central VLA training procedure. Student learning rates, batch sizes, trainable/frozen components, checkpoint initialization, and retention of earlier data during iterative refinement are insufficiently specified. Real-world relative-goal estimation is also unexplained. With no declared contribution type, I assess this as Algorithms/General: the promising integration and strong benchmark results make the decision close, but incomplete attribution of the proposed training contributions and limited comparative deployment evidence leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important visual-navigation problem: learning continuous control for cluttered, narrow, and dynamic environments from synthetic supervision. Under the default Algorithms/General category, the integration of specialized RL teachers, capability-balanced data aggregation, and multi-view VLA control constitutes a useful empirical contribution.

Public-benchmark results are strong. Table 1 reports 88.1% average success for multi-view MM-Nav versus 72.2% for SIDP. The single-view variant still achieves 83.3%, providing evidence that the improvement is not solely attributable to additional cameras.

The custom benchmark demonstrates substantial improvements in difficult settings: success increases over NavDP from 18% to 71% for squeezing, 27% to 68% for avoiding, and 23% to 47% in the mixed environment. Reporting collision rates alongside success helps assess navigation quality.

The ablations meaningfully investigate VQA co-training, camera coverage, iterative refinement, capability balancing, and expert combinations. Figure 7 supports improved learning of weaker capabilities under a fixed per-iteration sample budget, while Table 3 supports the benefit of combining complementary expert data.

Physical deployment strengthens the practical contribution. The VQA ablation includes 20 trials per model in each of four real-world scenarios, with large observed improvements. Reported 7 Hz execution and detailed RL configurations also provide useful implementation evidence.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is primarily in integration and training design: privileged-policy distillation, DAgger, VQA co-training, and temporal token pooling build on established approaches. The adaptive sampling rule is simple, and the 'unbalanced' comparator is insufficiently specified to establish its advantage over well-defined uniform or fixed-mixture sampling strategies.

The custom-benchmark comparisons conflate training methodology with camera coverage and control interfaces, as the paper itself attributes baseline failures partly to restricted fields of view. Single-view controls on this benchmark, or matched-input baselines trained on the expert data, would better isolate the proposed learning contribution. The public single-view results partially mitigate this concern.

Real-world evidence remains limited to four selected scenarios and comparison against the no-VQA variant, without competing navigation methods or detailed failure and intervention reporting. Thin-wire success is 55%, and simulation collision rates remain 20–32%. These results demonstrate promising transfer but support narrower robustness claims than the paper sometimes makes. Deployment also requires an external RTX 5090 server.

Several reporting inconsistencies need correction. Section 4.4 claims a VQA-removal performance drop exceeding 20% in both public-benchmark splits, which Table 1 does not support. Four refinement rounds imply 1.3 million navigation steps and 260,000 VQA examples, rather than the stated 1.5 million and 300,000. Table 3 also shows that the student does not exceed the squeezing teacher in success rate, so teacher-surpassing claims should specify the metric.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are incomplete. The manuscript omits important VLA optimization settings, precise VQA subset selection, and clear replay/aggregation details; the no-VQA row's camera configuration is also ambiguous. No repeated-training variability is reported, limiting confidence in smaller ablation differences. The latent-space visualizations are suggestive but do not independently establish the proposed mechanism of sim-to-real alignment.
